But once God is conceived in this way, the relationship Rûzbehân and the faithful of love experience between human and divine love becomes unthinkable. Divine love must be understood in the same way as divine knowledge. If God is the object of God’s own knowledge, and has revealed himself to himself in the divine Image—the primordial Human Form, the Anthropos, or heavenly Adam—in order to know himself within that Image by being known through it, then the Image’s knowledge of God must be precisely God’s knowledge of the Image.

In the same way, the love felt by this creature, which is God’s theophany and image, cannot be an event alien or external to the loving longing and ecstasy that the divinity experiences within itself for itself.

This is exactly the moving predicament into which the Book of the Clouding has brought us. It is altogether different from a theology calmly debating which attributes may or may not be assigned to its transcendent object. Here we experience the drama of divine love itself being played out in human love, because God’s revelation to himself through love takes place precisely through the trials and raptures of human love. Rûzbehân has described this contradiction within the divine with remarkable force.

From before eternity, God longs to be known; God yearns for a witness of contemplation (shâhid), yet immediately finds it intolerable that an Other should know and contemplate God. God therefore turns this Other away from knowing God, impelling the Other to know only itself rather than direct its gaze toward God. This is the great Trial of the Veil. Since, by essence, God can know only himself, the Witness’s knowledge of God must be none other than God’s own knowledge. The attainment of this transparency is experienced as victory over the Trial of the Veil.

The Witness then becomes God’s very act of contemplation—or rather the very eye through which God beholds himself. And it is through all these Witnesses, who in contemplating God are themselves those whom God contemplates—since God contemplates himself within them—that God looks upon the world. They are the eyes through which God contemplates himself. Such are the prophets, the abdâl (the spiritual “substitutes”), and the faithful of love: that small company who, in Sarî al-Saqatî’s account, withstand the sevenfold divine trial tempting them to “look away.”

To look away is to become conscious of oneself by losing oneself in an object—even paradise or hell—instead of recognizing oneself as the gaze through which God contemplates himself while contemplating them. Without these eyes, God would not see the world; for the world is that which has no eyes, and without this gaze it could not continue to exist. This drama of the shâhid, the Contemplator who is also the Contemplated, is the specifically Sufi orchestration of the Neoplatonic theme of the identity of love, lover, and beloved.

Since divine love is like divine knowledge, the same point must be made again. The Contemplated is the Contemplator; the act of contemplation is not other than what is contemplated. So it is with love, both in its act and in its object: the lover reveals himself to himself in the beloved, and, in return, the beloved reveals the lover to himself. This statement brings together all the stages through which the Book of Jasmine has led us. It makes that book the resolution of the problem, the answer to the Book of the Clouding, written “at the dictation of a wounded consciousness.”

The small band of mystical heroes who, in Sarî al-Saqatî’s story, survive the sevenfold trial because they have not “looked away” foreshadows the whole history of the faithful of love. They are “those to whom God communicates his secrets and who communicate their secrets to him.”
But God’s secrets and theirs are one and the same secret: the threefold identity of act, subject, and object.

It is human experience of love that gives us an intimation of this drama within the divine. At first a veil is cast, delaying self-revelation. The lover does not know that his love is what he himself is; he does not know that he is contemplating his own Image.

But to recognize it, he must pass beyond the limits both of a consciousness that turns everything into an object and of the carnal nature—the possessive instincts of the lower self. He must undergo a metamorphosis that changes the very subject within him, for the identity of love, lover, and beloved is precisely what divine love is. By undergoing this metamorphosis, human love fulfills the divinity’s own desire to have a shâhid, a witness of contemplation whose contemplation of the divine Essence is the divinity’s own.

In this way, human love truly becomes the path that makes divine love possible. Triumph over the “Trial of the Veil” is the joining of human love to divine love; it is divine love unveiled to itself as the human lover discovers the real divine Beloved. This is what it means to recognize a manifestation of divine beauty in human beauty. Human beauty thus initiates the mystical lover into the threefold identity of love, lover, and beloved; human love teaches him the solution to the equation.

The whole Sufi contemplative practice involving beautiful witnesses of contemplation rests on this assumption and pursues this end. And this is Rûzbehân’s great insight: it allows esoteric tawhîd to be expressed in the very language of love’s supreme experience, and makes that supreme experience the fulfillment of tawhîd.

To understand this, we need some knowledge of the three forms or degrees of tawhîd. The last, that of the “elect of the elect,” ends the divine anguish over the Other, because the deepest expression of the divine mystery can be glimpsed and experienced only through a tawhîd of love: the triumph of a higher, enduring existence that is itself a mystical death through love. Rûzbehân discusses these degrees at some length.

The first is what Sufism calls the tawhîd of ordinary people (tawhîd-e ’âmm): the abstract monotheism of ordinary, naïve, dogmatic faith, which is satisfied only when the Divine has been completely objectified. It sets the Ens supremum, a single transcendent Supreme Being, above the totality of created beings. It constructs proofs and arguments for God’s existence, seeking shelter in them against the shocks of doubt and the risk of denial. Its overriding concern is which Attributes may be assigned to a divine Essence set apart from creatures and becoming. It proceeds by stripping away (tanzîh), haunted by the twin dangers of anthropomorphism (tashbîh) and excessive abstraction (ta’til). Having removed the divine object from every category of created existence, it believes it has safeguarded God’s transcendence.

Yet these rational purifications have made God into precisely the kind of object that serves a “sociomorphic” religion—a religion that conceives the divine relationship on the model of social relations. Once the Divine is turned into an object, it is also socialized. Every free spiritual movement, such as Sufism, that discovers contact between human and divine in the depths of personal consciousness becomes suspect.

The totality of beings, gathered on a level plane and held at an equal distance from the transcendent object by its all-encompassing claim, could be represented by a formula such as n + 1. For Sufism, as for Ismailism, this ordinary tawhîd never ceases committing the very metaphysical idolatry it so deeply fears.

There is next the tawhîd already called that of the elect, a special tawhîd (tawhîd-e khâss). The affirmation of the One moves from the assertion of one unique transcendent object to the affirmation of the unity of being. All beings are experienced as vanishing before the sublimity of the one Being, as mere negations in relation to its divine lordship (robbîya). Before eternity, God was and nothing else was; even now, nothing has changed.

All existence is immersed in the divine reality (res divina, amr ilâhî) through an intuitive vision that replaces rational knowledge, “for rational knowledge belongs to ordinary people, whereas intuitive vision is the prerogative of the initiated (khawâss).” The tawhîd of ordinary people keeps company with the intellect’s proofs and the objects it constructs. For the initiated, all these proofs disappear, and they themselves disappear from those proofs and objectifications. They experience their own passing away, their fanâ’, within the divine abiding existence, whose attributes alone remain. If the idea of fanâ’ is made commonplace, we arrive at that all-too-easy, tiresomely familiar picture of mystical experience as the dissolution of individual personality.

So caricatured, it is no less naïve than the tawhîd of ordinary believers: it simply replaces n + 1 with something like the sterile equation 1 = 1. Unable to recognize appearances as apparitions—as things through which the divine appears—the metaphysical identity it constructs is no less illusory than the metaphysical illusions it denounces. In fact, for our Sufis this second degree of tawhîd, corresponding to the experience of fanâ’, is only the passage toward a third form, which brings about the annihilation of annihilation itself.
As Rûzbehân emphasizes, the first tawhîd proceeds from the visible world toward God (az ’âlam-e molk be-Haqq). The second proceeds from the personal self toward God (az khwôd be-Haqq).

But there is a third, which proceeds from God to God (az Haqq be-Haqq). It never leaves God: it takes place within the divinity itself. And because it takes place within the divinity, the secret of human love belongs within the very mystery of divine love and brings that mystery to fulfillment. This is the tawhîd of the elect of the elect (tawhîd-e khâss-e khâss). It involves a double negation: the annihilation of the annihilation achieved by the second degree. All the forms submerged by that second degree in the undifferentiated identity of God now rise again, resurrected and restored.

But the perspective is reversed: “Below becomes above, and above becomes below.” Rûzbehân says further: “It means casting oneself into the sea of nonbeing, but in order to be annihilated to nothingness—or to annihilate nothingness within oneself. It means emerging from the sea of abiding existence (baqâ’).

“Henceforth the mystic sees, without himself—that is, having been carried outside himself—God through God (bi-khwôd Haqq-râ be-Haqq binad).” He sees, certainly, yet it is not he who sees. It is God who sees through him. He is the eye through which God contemplates himself. This is what “above has become below” means, and vice versa: “He knows that this is one step from nonbeing into being.
“The second step carries him from the servile human condition (bandagî) on the wing of divine lordship (robbîyat), into the free expanse of divine Selfhood (howîyat).”

This second step transforms his condition from that of an object subject to a power (maqdarî) into that of a subject possessing power (qâdir). It is a transmutation of his very subjectivity. In understanding that he is “the eye through which God sees himself,” he knows himself to be divine knowledge, divine hearing, and so forth. All the forms, all the theophanies, have risen again from the abyss of undifferentiation.

Yet the mystic’s “Holy Spirit” sees that every Attribute he contemplates is the very eye through which God contemplates him. “You must travel, journey through the being of being, with and as the divine Gaze, until being disappears into being for you. Then, without you—that is, with you outside yourself, absent from yourself—the vision of vision (’ayn-e ’iyân) blossoms within you.

“When you reach that point, after the two stages of effacement and recovered consciousness, your very existence proclaims through each of its atoms: ‘I am God.’ To be annihilated in the sea of abiding existence is to annihilate annihilation within yourself, to be annihilated to nothingness—or to have nothingness annihilated. Then, yes, God grants you the being of a divine eye (dîdeh-hastî, so that you see each being as a divine eye).

“God clothes you in the robe of abiding existence: to abide through God’s life, to live from that life, to live within that life. It is through God and in God that you contemplate—that is, your gaze is God’s own gaze contemplating itself. This is the secret of lordship (sirr-e robbîyat), the very secret of tawhîd.”

To see that your own gaze is the eye through which the Divine Being contemplates himself: this is what Rûzbehân calls the vision of vision. The Image has itself become a mirror. It reveals its secret to the person who sees it, for in seeing it that person sees himself; and as the Image sees him, he sees himself seeing himself outside himself. This resolves the conflict Rûzbehân has repeatedly felt in his visions between the oneness of the pure divine Essence and the multiplicity of theophanies—a conflict that surfaced in his consciousness as an anxious question. It cannot be resolved if its terms are treated as objects that can be added together or reduced to an undifferentiated unity.
We can represent ordinary tawhîd as n + 1, and the second degree as 1 = 1.

But Rûzbehân has already suggested the formula corresponding to the third degree: “Until he becomes the product of unity multiplied by unity (wâhid dar wâhid, 1 × 1), the mystical pilgrim does not attain the vision of the vision of tawhîd.” (In musical terms, think of the relationship of the octave within the upper harmonic series.) This expresses precisely the relationship between unity and the multiplicity of theophanies. It is realized each time—kath’héna—as unity multiplies itself by itself, the same gaze multiplying itself by itself: unity of unity, vision of vision. For each time, the one contemplated is the contemplator’s own gaze.

Esoteric tawhîd thus expresses exactly the unity that brings love, lover, and beloved together, at the moment when human love, in supreme clarity, becomes the revealer of divine love. This is the passage from love still understood metaphorically (’ishq majâzî, because it sees only the outward or “literal” form) to love in its true sense (haqîqî, because it sees what is invisible within that form).

The identity affirmed by the Neoplatonic formula is not, then, an identity belonging uniquely to a transcendent object set above other objects. It expresses the very essence of love, whose underlying principle is the same in its divine and its human forms. Human love is an intimation of divine love and the path toward it. It is its initiation and therefore its first realization, for through human love the veil falls from the mystery of the Contemplator-Contemplated.

Addressing the beautiful woman for whom he wrote the Book of Jasmine—who is herself his shâhid—Rûzbehân writes: “Such is the story of the faithful of love, O flame that draws the souls of men of longing as a flame draws moths! … If we ourselves are not love, lover, and beloved, then who is? Everything outside this indivisible instant belongs only to the world of duality, the world of objects.

“Ponder this strange thing: it is I myself who, without myself—that is, with myself absent, outside myself—am the lover of myself (man bar man bi-mân ’âshiq-am). I never cease to contemplate myself, without myself, in the mirror that is the beloved’s existence. Then who am I?” Here, in this tawhîd of love, we find the very terms and paradoxical turn of phrase that express the secret of esoteric tawhîd.

The gaze the lover contemplates in the mirror is his own gaze. At the same time it is not his, because it is the gaze of the other; and yet this Other is himself. The vision of vision: this is what the Sufis would meditate upon endlessly in the exemplary story of Majnûn and Layla—the “Tristan and Isolde” of their mystical epic. Rûzbehân seals his statement of the tawhîd of love with these four verses:

In search of Jamshîd’s Grail, I traveled the world. Not for a day did I rest, not for a night did I sleep. But when I heard the Master describe the Grail of Jamshîd, That Grail which reveals the universe—behold, it was myself.

And Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator, to whom we owe so much illumination of difficult chapters of the Jasmine, quietly draws out what matters most: “When the mystic reaches perfection in love,” he says, “he brings together within himself two modes of being: that of the lover (’âshiq) and that of the beloved (ma’shûq). Then he cries: I am the one I love, and the one I love is me; we are two spirits dwelling within a single body. This is the authentic interpretation of this mystical station: the lover’s person is the dwelling place of two spirits.

“The language of the religion of love has a special beauty and elegance for those who understand it, in calling the mode of being of the lover, of the beloved, and of love itself a spirit (rûh). When this spiritual state reaches the utmost limit of perfection, God himself, through his own eternal gaze, contemplates his own eternal face. Then the existence of my own human reality no longer enters into it. And that is exactly what the venerable shaykh means when he says: it is I myself who, without myself—or outside myself—am the lover of myself.”

The subject of vision is the same in esoteric tawhîd and in the supreme tawhîd of love. In esoteric tawhîd, Rûzbehân told us, the mystic henceforth sees God through God, “outside” himself (bi-khwôd); he is the very gaze with which God sees himself. In the tawhîd of love, his commentator has just told us that God himself contemplates his eternal face with his own gaze.

The identity of these statements conveys Rûzbehân’s entire teaching in a few words: the relationship he establishes between human and divine love, in which the latter brings the former to its utmost perfection. This teaching distinguishes the faithful of love from the “pious devotees,” whose spiritual path knows nothing of initiation through human love. Speaking again of the faithful lover who reaches the utmost perfection, Rûzbehân says: “He is the Desiring and the Desired, the Lover and the Beloved.

“In relation to God he assumes the role of witness of contemplation—the shâhid in whom God contemplates himself. It is God who contemplates himself in that person with an eternal gaze.” This is the meaning of the vision of vision, of 1 × 1; and it is the meaning of the Qur’anic verse: “Light upon light” (24:35).

In the mystical lover’s supreme state, the Divine Being’s longing to have a witness of contemplation who is no other than himself is fulfilled. Divine jealousy vanishes before the transparency of this pure Witness, whose gaze is God’s own. This is what the story of Majnûn exemplifies. It is therefore true to say that the supreme ecstasy of Majnûn’s human love is the mystery of divine love made transparent. It answers and fulfills that mystery, since from before eternity it was in human form that God revealed divine beauty to himself.

The drama of God’s jealous longing, shown to us in the Book of the Clouding, thus finds its resolution in the extreme ecstasy of Majnûn’s love. Human and divine love are therefore not opposed to each other. The passage from one to the other is an initiation into love’s true meaning and perfection, and this initiation is indispensable. It is not a passage from one object to another, from an object that is not God to an object that is God.

When Majnûn’s love reaches its supreme ecstasy, he becomes a witness of contemplation for God himself. He becomes, in Rûzbehân’s words, the “mirror of God” (mir’ât-e Haqq), the mirror in which God contemplates himself and is revealed to himself. Majnûn has overcome the Trial of the Veil. This is why divine love can contemplate itself only in someone like Majnûn, and why Rûzbehân built his mystical teaching upon this experience of human love.
7. The “history” of the faithful of love

The last elements of our final theme now fall into place. Because this is the relationship of human love to divine longing, which aspires to reveal itself to itself; because it is in the mystical lover that the Divine Being finds a pure mirror, an eye directed toward God that is God’s own gaze—the Trial of the Veil is necessary.

God must bring before the earthly lover a beautiful face which, by becoming the lover’s witness of contemplation, will initiate him into a transformation of vision. He will learn to discover in the beauty of that face a theophany of eternal Beauty. By overcoming the Trial of the Veil, the mystical lover discovers that his contemplation is the Divine Being’s contemplation of himself through the gaze that belongs to him.
Thus some have been able to say that it is God who loves himself in Majnûn’s love for Layla.

Someone uninitiated into this experience might hear the Neoplatonic formula as an expression of solipsism, abolishing the energetic tension between subject and object on which love depends. The truth is exactly the opposite. The Neoplatonic statement describes a real polarity, the polarity of a two-in-one unity. If its object remained external, love’s spiritual energy would eventually be exhausted.

But when that energy is drawn into the mutual inwardness of lover and beloved, it grows more intense and multiplies itself. Love is driven by ardent longing, and longing only increases with love, because love is what makes us see, and the power of vision increases with love. “Ardent longing is further strengthened by the Spirit’s flight,” Rûzbehân writes.

“The higher it flies, the greater the longing becomes, because in the mirage of dazzling light, thirst itself is the longing to feel thirst. In the religion of the faithful of love, there is never a final attainment of union, though there is never separation either, because the laws of time do not apply to what is eternal. The soul, while longing, is granted a vision of Majesty.
“But the very act of seeing only melts the heart into still greater ardor, because longing never ceases to yearn for vision.”

But if the lover is identical with the beloved, Rûzbehân continues, what can he still long for? What can his love be the love of, other than himself? (To ask the question in this way is to confuse what the formulas 1 = 1 and 1 × 1 represent. Needless to say, the confusion is common.) No, Rûzbehân replies: this is the moment to reflect on the Qur’anic verse, “They have not measured God with the measure due to him” (6:91).

For this is what love means: to be two. What we must understand, however, is the kind of two-ness implied by the essential unity of love, lover, and beloved. It is a two-ness for which we shall once again translate the Persian du’î as dualitude, not duality: a One and a One which, in multiplying one another, are One.

For esoteric tawhîd and the tawhîd of love are the unity of Contemplator and Contemplated, of lover and beloved. That is why “Love, the rider mounted on Longing, travels as far as the sea of tawhîd, but no farther. Beyond that point, neither love nor longing would remain.” To go farther would be to pass beyond the mystery of the divine revealing itself to itself within this unity.

“But love advances by longing; only in this vessel does it reach the shores of vision”—on the sea of tawhîd. And because the lover must reach those shores if God is to find a witness of contemplation in him, God causes the vision to rise before the sanctuary of his soul. Then “this man of longing becomes the partner of a bride like you. For those who seek intimacy with God, you are the place of intimacy; for those who truly understand what moves their longing, you are the flower blooming in the garden of mystical knowledge.”

Rûzbehân has already taught us what it means to be a “partner.” The existence of the theophanic universe depends on him, in the sense that it rests with him to recognize human beauty as a manifestation of divine beauty. In turn, by bringing her partner to this recognition, the beauty that reveals God initiates him into recognizing the face Rûzbehân calls the Eternal Bride (’arûs-e qidam), until he sees that face alone in the mirror of the transient world.

This is the whole love story of Majnûn and Layla, to which we have already alluded so often and which our Sufis never tired of pondering. The transformation Majnûn undergoes through his love for Layla is precisely what finally makes him a witness of contemplation, the “Mirror of God.” His passion is understood as the mystical death through love that makes possible the advent of the vision of vision, the tawhîd of the “elect of the elect.”

In South Arabia, in Yemen, there once existed—or at least poetic tradition imagines there existed—an ideal tribe renowned for its practice of a chaste, Platonic love known as ’odhrîte love. Poets celebrated its famous pairs of lovers; Rûzbehân names several at the beginning of his Jasmine. Majnûn and Layla would be the North Arabian counterparts of these ideal lovers celebrated by the poets of South Arabia. They have counterparts, too—perhaps even predecessors—in the Persian mystical epic, where the theme has survived into modern times.

We need not enter here into the extremely complex question of its historical origins. What matters for our present purpose is to bring out certain differences. Despite the similarities, Majnûn’s case is distinct from those of his counterparts, the heroes of ’odhrîte love.

Moreover, although it was indeed through Sufi reflection that Majnûn came to be regarded as an exemplary hero of pure love, there is a difference between the way certain Sufi masters before Rûzbehân used his story in their preaching and the significance Rûzbehân gives it. That significance follows directly from Rûzbehân’s understanding of human love as an initiation into divine love, and as the lived experience, at its highest perfection, of what esoteric tawhîd implies. This interpretation bears the deep imprint of Iranian Sufism. It defines those whom, following Rûzbehân, we call the faithful of love, distinguishing them from pious devotees and ascetic devotees (zohhâd).
Two features characterize Majnûn’s love as the Sufis understood it, and together they are enough to distinguish it from ’odhrîte love in the ordinary sense.

First, Majnûn’s consciousness is so completely absorbed by the thought and image of Layla that every other feeling is banished. Ask him about Layla, and he answers, “I am Layla.” Ask his name or how he is, and he gives the same answer. More than that, he perceives the entire outer world through this image. Whether he sees a wild animal, a mountain, a flower, or a human being, the same word rises to his lips to identify it: Layla.

Second—and this is surely the underlying condition of such a state of consciousness—Majnûn has completely internalized the beloved’s person. It goes so far that he no longer desires Layla’s physical presence, for fear she would distract him from his love for the Layla within him, more real than the real Layla. These two characteristics describe an experience of love not necessarily implied by the definition of ’odhrîte love.

In any event, this total absorption in the beloved’s inward presence is why Sufi masters such as Shiblî (861–945 CE) present Majnûn in their sermons as the model of the true mystic, whose consciousness is so utterly absorbed in God that he knows himself and perceives the outer world only through God. For how could a mystic claim to love God while remaining able to distinguish and take as his own the trivial certainties of ordinary consciousness? On this point the Sufis certainly recognized in Majnûn something different from simple ’odhrîte love.

Yet they still treated him as a model, an example. It is as though the mystic were merely being invited to love God as Majnûn loves Layla. One could then perfectly well remain within an understanding of God as an object, and imagine “conversion” to divine love as the transfer of love from one object, Layla, to another, God.

But what Rûzbehân has taught us about human love initiating us into divine love is something quite different, and it reveals what is essential to the originality of his Sufism. First, Majnûn’s love for Layla must be understood as the path of access to divine love.

Second, the dawning of divine love must not be imagined as the transfer of affection from one object to another; it is a metamorphosis in which Majnûn becomes a mirror where the Divine Being contemplates himself and finds a shâhid. As to the first point, we have heard Rûzbehân say to the beloved: “It is impossible to cross the rushing river—the Jayhân—of tawhîd without the bridge of your love.”

But crossing that bridge is not simply moving from a human object to a divine one. It means passing through a metamorphosis that overturns the very idea of an object. “Above becomes below; below becomes above.” The transformation is so complete that it speaks in paradoxes and ecstatic outcries (shathîyât) that scandalize the conventionally devout.

For Rûzbehân, Majnûn is far more than a model whose example needs only to be transposed into the practice of divine love. Majnûn’s condition has made him the “Mirror of God.” And what is that, if not divine love itself? It means that his very being has become the eye (dîdeh-hastî!) through which God looks upon himself. He could not say “I am Layla” in the way he does unless he had become that mirror.

If Majnûn experiences himself as Layla, it is because he has himself become the “mirror of God,” or the “eye of God” revealing himself to himself in Layla’s beauty. His extravagant outcry of ecstatic love thus answers the question Rûzbehân asked his interlocutor in the prologue to the Jasmine: “As God contemplates himself in you, contemplates the eternal Face in the beauty of your face, who then are you?” Majnûn’s outcry presupposes that he has crossed the torrent of tawhîd by the bridge of love for Layla. That is the crossing itself, the blossoming of human love into divine love.

Rûzbehân and his commentator have told us that when the mystical lover’s human love reaches this supreme ecstasy, it is God who, in the lover’s gaze, contemplates God’s own eternal face through God’s own gaze. And it is precisely upon reaching the vision of vision that Hallâj’s famous ecstatic declaration is uttered: “I am God.”

Rûzbehân instructs the mystic: “When you have attained the vision of vision, every atom of your being proclaims: I am God.” For then “every atom of creation is an eye of God.” Recall everything he has taught us about the way the beauty of the shâhid reveals God—Layla being Majnûn’s shâhid—and we can understand why Rûzbehân and his commentator describe in the same terms the mystical state expressed both in Majnûn’s outcry and in that of Hallâj.

Each is a vision of vision. In it the mystical lover, outside himself, carried beyond himself (bi-khwôd), sees his own gaze as the gaze with which God contemplates himself. The theophanic Image is the organ of this vision of vision. The Image’s complete inward presence is, as it were, balanced by the mystic’s being placed “outside himself,” his departure from himself, his ek-stasis.

Because the vision of vision requires this ek-stasis of ecstatic love, producing the perfect transparency that makes Majnûn the eye and mirror through which God contemplates himself, it presupposes the “annihilation of annihilation” that constitutes the third degree of tawhîd. The movement of the subject “outside himself” demanded by esoteric tawhîd therefore appears spontaneously as the “mystical death through love,” of which Majnûn is again the perfect embodiment. Now the prophetic saying we encountered earlier takes on its full meaning: “Whoever loves, remains chaste, and dies having kept his secret dies as a true witness.” For Majnûn’s ecstatic love is, in the fullest sense, an initiatory death.

Here we see all the technical terms in the language of the faithful of love meet and cross. The witness of contemplation (shâhid) becomes the true witness (shahîd, “martyr”). The place of his witness-bearing—the place of his “martyrdom,” mashhad—is the place where divine Beauty appears (mazhar): the beautiful being who is its theophany. The same word, mashhad, has also been explained to us earlier as a name for paradise. Rûzbehân’s whole teaching about the divine appearing in beauty aims at this transubstantiation of the contemplative lover into a pure mirror, so that he endures as witness to the Absolute, as the very eye with which the Absolute contemplates itself.

The final pages of the Jasmine now sound like a finale, allusively bringing together every theme of the book. Rûzbehân quotes Sanâ’î, that other great Persian mystical poet (d. ca. 535/1141), several times. Following him, he repeats:
Let the sword of love wound you So that you may find eternal Life, For at the stroke of Azrael’s blade, No one shows any sign of rising again.

This means that physical death, the exitus, is neither the prelude to resurrection nor its announcement. Only initiatory death opens the way to it. That is how our Sufis understand mystical death through love, for “love does not accept a soul that it would leave alive”—alive, that is, in its former life.

Yet “for someone whose only guide is love, unbelief and orthodoxy are alike a veil blocking the threshold. Everything partial or total among beings forms the arch of a bridge on the path of love.” “Alone with God, I taste the moment reserved for those who transcend ordinary humanity.” Rûzbehân presses Sanâ’î’s fearless words still further: “For the faithful of love there is no false religion and no heresy; neither immorality nor naïve innocence exists for them. … Paradise is the dwelling place of pious devotees. The Fire Temple is the mystical tavern of the faithful of love.

“Love does not tolerate immaturity. The path of love does not tolerate weakness.” This mystical death, he says again, is the lover’s complete assimilation to love, that is, “to the substance of love, which is coeternal with the soul.” To translate his terms (yakrangî, ham-rangî) fully, we would need to coin words such as symmorphosis and synchromatism: a transformation that makes the lover conform to love, accomplished in four phases parallel to those leading to esoteric tawhîd.

“All that we have just said,” Rûzbehân writes, “does no more than describe the state of being of love and of the faithful lover. The outermost limit of love is the beginning of mystical knowledge (ma’rifat). In mystical knowledge, love reaches its highest perfection. If the Lover becomes of one color (ham-rang) with the Beloved, he has attained the mystical station of tawhîd. If he is struck with wonder in mystical knowledge, he has attained the station of that knowledge. These two stations mark the furthest reach of love.

“When he has become a perfect knower of the divine, the divine Attributes appear to him through the attributes of his own mystical knowledge. To remember the Essence and meditate upon the Attributes is still to advance with modest restraint in the footsteps of eternal Wisdom.
“But the coming together of the Lover’s gaze—or person, jam’-e ’ayn—with the gaze—or person—of the Beloved is contained within the unifying gaze (’ayn-e jam’) that is love’s very essence.

“Thus, when love blossoms in a being, it draws that being toward this union of gazes. Through four phases—the annihilation of his own actions and qualities; the annihilation of that annihilation; the abiding existence of both; and the abiding of that abiding existence—the Lover becomes the Beloved.

“In the kingdom of divine lordship he possesses the divine mode of being and experiences supreme felicity. Then, if his love, a royal falcon, carries him to the vision of tawhîd, the mystical lover knows the joy of the One who reaches the goal: he contemplates the eye that contemplates him (shohûd-e ’ayn), as though he himself were that eye.”

Now we can also understand fully the words of Rûzbehân’s anonymous commentator, whom we must quote one last time. They seem to sum up the entire doctrine of theophany by describing three mirrors of contemplation. There is, he tells us, “1) The mirror in which to contemplate what is invisible, hidden, esoteric in the Divine Being: the three organs of subtle perception—the heart, the innermost secret (sirr), and the spirit. 2) The mirror in which to contemplate what is outward, manifest, the visible form of God, the divine as it appears (sûrat-e Haqq): the external senses, the faculties of sensory perception illuminated by the three subtle organs. 3) The mirror in which to contemplate God’s eternal Face: human eyes illuminated by love.”

This is why, if so many of Rûzbehân’s statements have reminded us of a central teaching of Meister Eckhart—“the gaze by which I know Him is the very gaze by which He knows me”—we must add that Rûzbehân of Shîrâz would be a Meister Eckhart who had also written the romance of Tristan and Isolde.

We would thereby identify the twofold character of the Iranian mystical genius as it speaks both in its vast mystical epics and in Sufism, from Sanâ’î in the eleventh century to Nûr ’Alî-Shâh in the nineteenth. Our philosophies have recast the relationship between God and the world in social terms, whether to affirm or deny that relationship.

But the sense of the divine that we learn from this Sufism is not of a God who governs the world. It is of a divinity revealed to the intuition of the heart through the love awakened there by divine manifestations in beauty. This is perhaps the supreme paradox bequeathed by that Sufism to a world which may seem to us, even more than it did to Rûzbehân, a world “without eyes”—and therefore a world that God does not look upon, that God is not “concerned” with.

We have heard Rûzbehân’s anxious question during one of his visions: Where were You yesterday during the spiritual concert (samâ’), that I did not see You? This question, “Where are you?”, is one we hear these seekers after God asking, one after another, down through the centuries; for the matter so deeply “concerns” them. We hear it, among other places, in a very simple and moving poem by Fakhroddîn ’Erâqî (d. ca. 686/1287), one of the most celebrated poets of Iranian Sufism and a disciple of Sadroddîn Qonyawî. It was under Qonyawî’s influence that he became passionately devoted to Ibn ’Arabî’s mystical theosophy.

Love for you has driven me out of my senses. Where are you? With all my soul I seek you, O soul of mine. Where are you? I travel the world in search of you. Everywhere I seek you. Where are you? Since the world cannot contain your beauty, How could I know what you are like, or where you are? Since no one can pass into the place where you are, Whom shall I ask? Who could know where you are? You are manifest, yet hidden from everyone. And if you are not hidden, where do you appear? … To my startled and bewildered heart, Give a sign along the Way. Where are you? Since poor ’Erâqî is beside himself because of you, Will you not at last say to him: O madman of love, where are you?

What a revealing poem. The question “Where are you?” turns back upon itself. The person who asks it longs to hear it addressed to himself. For if he does hear it, he will at last have heard the answer to his own question. In other words, the poem announces that mysterious reversal of vision in which the Contemplator discovers that, in the very act of contemplation, he is himself the Contemplated: the Cogito (“I think”) becomes a Cogitor (“I am thought”).

The Book of Jasmine closes upon this mystery. Rûzbehân takes leave of the woman at whose request he wrote the book, recalling one last time the divine manifestations that can be read in the beauty of her face—provided one reads with the eyes of the soul. For him this beauty is what the vision of the Angel descending toward the horizon and “remaining suspended” there (Qur’an 53:8) was for the Prophet. As the manifestation of the divine Attribute above all others, it is itself the very eye through which the person who witnesses it contemplates it.

“All that we have just said is the history of the faithful of love, those who love with a spiritual and divine love. O you whose eyes are like jasmine; you who bear upon your face the secret of the divine self-manifestations (sirr-e af’âl); you whose blinking eyelids threaten the unique faithful of love with the sorcery of Hârût and Mârût; you whose love is the center of the imperishable heaven, though it holds a thousand complaints and laments over the transient world in store for the faithful of love; you whose brow reveals hundreds of theophanies to those who look with the eyes of the soul, while the gracious feints of your gaze give the understanding hundreds of occasions to remain suspended (53:8) beneath the very eye of the theophany! Only one who shares the inconsolable heart’s condition can know its inmost state.

“Let us say it plainly: the lamp of the divine Attributes is set in the Niche of the visible Signs. In this chapter the faithful of love will find many allusions to that mystery. In the following couplet by the wondrous mystical lover, that royal creature of ardent longing, Hosayn ibn Mansûr al-Hallâj, we find a similar ecstatic outcry, rich with hidden indications. He uttered it in the intoxication of tawhîd, under the influence of a gaze that discerned Unity, while his blood was flowing and he recited:
Glory to Him who revealed His humanity As the glorious mystery of His radiant divinity, And then appeared openly within His creature In the form of one who eats and drinks.

The moment when the Contemplator becomes the Contemplated, when the one asking “Where are you?” hears that very question addressed to himself, is the moment when he penetrates the secret of the famous saying: “Whoever knows himself knows his Lord.” And then he also understands the mystical meaning of the Qur’anic summons: “O soul at peace, return to your Lord, well pleased and pleasing to Him.”
